prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- British Airways is asking thousands of its staff to work for free for up to four weeks, spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday. British Airways plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. In an e-mail to all its staff, the airline offered workers between one and four weeks of unpaid leave -- but with the option to work during this period. British Airways employs just more than 40,000 people in the United Kingdom. Last month, the company posted a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million). Its chief executive declared at the time there were "absolutely no signs of recovery" in the industry. "In 30 years in this business and I've never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced," said Willie Walsh, British Airways' chief executive.  Watch more about BA's request » . A spokesman for one of Britain's biggest unions said its workers could not afford to work for free for a month. "It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year," said Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite. He pointed out that the airline was not ordering staff to work without pay. "It's a request -- you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave." Demand for the airline's passenger seats and cargo holds fell during the last financial year, while its fuel bill rocketed to almost £3 billion ($4.7 billion). Walsh said British Airways' woes were inextricably linked to the downturn in the global economy and that there had been no sign of any "green shoots" of recovery. Like its premium-class competitors, British Airways is losing customers to cheaper rivals. The airline's premium passenger numbers fell 13 percent in the second half of last year, in line with the industry average. Total traffic fell 3.4 percent and while the airline carried 33.1 million passengers last year, it was a drop of 4.3 percent from the previous year. The dip in demand for British Airways' flights has forced a switch in strategy at the airline. From the end of last year, it has been trying to tempt passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat for "bums on seats." It plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. CNN's Alysen Miller contributed to this report.

**LONDON, England (CNN) —** British Airways is asking thousands of employees to work without pay for up to four weeks, spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday.

The airline plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. In an email to all employees, British Airways offered workers between one and four weeks of unpaid leave, with the option of continuing to work during that period.

British Airways employs just over 40,000 people in the United Kingdom. Last month, the company reported a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million). At the time, its chief executive said there were “absolutely no signs of recovery” in the industry.

“In 30 years in this business, I’ve never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced,” said Willie Walsh, British Airways’ chief executive.

*Watch more about BA’s request »*

A spokesman for one of Britain’s largest unions said its members could not afford to work without pay for a month.

“It’s all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he’s prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year,” said Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite.

Naidoo emphasized that the airline was not ordering employees to work without pay.

“It’s a request—you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave.”

Demand for the airline’s passenger seats and cargo capacity declined during the last financial year, while its fuel bill soared to nearly £3 billion ($4.7 billion).

Walsh said British Airways’ difficulties were inextricably linked to the global economic downturn and that there had been no sign of any “green shoots” of recovery.

Like its premium-class competitors, British Airways is losing customers to lower-cost rivals. The airline’s premium passenger numbers fell 13 percent in the second half of last year, in line with the industry average.

Total traffic declined 3.4 percent. Although the airline carried 33.1 million passengers last year, that figure represented a 4.3 percent drop from the previous year.

The decline in demand for British Airways flights has forced the airline to change its strategy. Since the end of last year, it has sought to attract passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat in favor of putting more “bums on seats.”

The airline plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft.

CNN’s Alysen Miller contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**LONDON, England (CNN) —** British Airways has invited thousands of employees to give up their pay for as long as a month while continuing to work, company spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday.

The proposal was sent by e-mail to the airline’s entire workforce. Employees were offered one to four weeks of unpaid leave, with the choice of still reporting for work during that time. British Airways has slightly more than 40,000 employees in the United Kingdom.

The request comes after the carrier announced a record full-year loss of £400 million ($656 million) last month. At the time, Chief Executive Willie Walsh said the aviation sector showed “absolutely no signs of recovery.”

“In 30 years in this business and I've never seen anything like this,” Walsh said. “This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced.”

*Watch more about BA’s request »*

Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite, one of Britain’s largest labor unions, said employees could not afford to go without a month’s salary.

“It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year,” Naidoo said.

He emphasized, however, that the company was making a voluntary request rather than instructing employees to work without compensation.

“It's a request — you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave,” he said.

During the most recent financial year, demand declined for both passenger seats and cargo space, while British Airways’ fuel costs surged to nearly £3 billion ($4.7 billion).

Walsh said the carrier’s difficulties were inseparable from the worldwide economic downturn and added that there were no “green shoots” indicating a recovery.

As with other airlines focused on premium travel, British Airways has been losing business to less expensive competitors. Premium-passenger totals dropped by 13 percent in the second half of last year, matching the average decline across the industry.

Overall traffic decreased by 3.4 percent. The airline transported 33.1 million travelers last year, 4.3 percent fewer than in the preceding year.

Weakening demand has also prompted British Airways to alter its business approach. Beginning at the end of last year, the carrier started using lower ticket prices to attract customers, accepting less profit from each seat in exchange for putting more “bums on seats.”

For next winter, British Airways intends to cut capacity by 4 percent and may take as many as 16 aircraft out of service.

CNN’s Alysen Miller contributed to this report.

outputs.L4:
British Airways has asked more than 40,000 employees in the United Kingdom to take between one and four weeks of unpaid leave as it struggles with a record £400 million annual loss, weakening demand and sharply higher fuel costs. Under the proposal, staff may take the time off or continue working without pay, an unusual option that highlights the depth of the airline’s financial difficulties.

The request forms part of a broader effort to reduce costs and match operations to declining passenger and freight volumes. British Airways plans to cut capacity by about 4 percent and could park as many as 16 aircraft. The company has said that voluntary measures are needed to preserve cash and limit the impact of the downturn.

Trade unions reacted critically, arguing that most employees could not afford to give up several weeks of pay. While some senior executives might be able to make such a sacrifice, union representatives said the proposal was financially unrealistic for lower-paid staff and risked placing an unfair share of the burden on workers.

The airline’s problems reflect a wider crisis across the aviation industry. The recession has reduced leisure travel, cargo shipments and, most damagingly, demand from premium passengers. Numbers traveling in first and business class have fallen by around 13 percent, depriving airlines of a particularly important source of revenue.

With fuel costs remaining high and no clear signs of a recovery in demand, British Airways faces continued pressure to reduce spending and shrink its schedule. The appeal for unpaid leave, together with the capacity cuts and planned grounding of aircraft, demonstrates how severely the economic downturn has affected both the carrier and the global airline sector.
